newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Energy Dept. has plan to monitor nuclear arms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Energy Dept. has plan to monitor nuclear arms.

text.p: The Energy Department on Tuesday announced plans for a $4 billion-a-year program to manage the nation's nuclear weapons stockpile, but critics called it a bloated, dangerous scheme.
The department's plan called for shrinking weapons manufacturing operations at facilities in Oak Ridge, Tenn., Kansas City, Mo., and Amarillo, Texas.

To maintain and check the stockpile without underground nuclear testing, the plan called for building two new facilities at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California and a facility at the Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico.
The plan also would re-establish, but on a smaller scale, the capability to make the plutonium core of nuclear weapons at Los Alamos, which the department said would "support the existing stockpile."
The Clinton administration has said it was committed to keeping a nuclear arsenal to deter threats from other countries, but without developing new weapons and without underground testing.

"Cutting-edge science and technology will support the shift from weapons design and production to maintaining the safety and reliability of the nuclear stockpile without underground testing," Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary said in a statement.

But the Military Production Network, a coalition of environmental and anti-nuclear groups, said it planned to sue to block the department from carrying out the plan that it said would allow the department "to spend $40 billion over the next 10 years on dangerous, irrelevant programs."
Maureen Eldredge, of the organization, said the new facilities could harm the surrounding environment and produce dangerous waste.
Eldredge also said high-tech methods the department intended to use to check the stockpile without underground testing could be used by other countries to help develop their nuclear weapons.
"We see these kind of investments in new technologies in virtual testing and virtual bomb development as being a significant risk for the non-proliferation regime," she said.
The plan for monitoring the stockpile would use three new supercomputers and facilities for fabricating nuclear detonation, and sites for high explosive testing.
Environmental groups had called for more shrinking of the weapons operations and said the department did not adequately consider alternatives to its initial proposals.
But department officials in a telephone briefing said the alternatives did not meet the tests of ensuring national security or were not technically feasible.
They also defended the program's pricetag, which some critics said nearly matched the Cold War years.

"There's a considerable amount of nuclear weapons that we have to maintain. While the numbers are down, trying to do that without nuclear testing is just a very difficult job and you're supposed to do that indefinitely," said Vic Reis, assistant energy secretary for defense programs.
